questions.question: What are the three steps in the CPU's core execution cycle?
options: Read, Write, Delete
Fetch, Decode, Execute
Load, Store, Jump
Input, Process, Output
questions.explanation: The CPU continuously performs the fetch-decode-execute cycle: it fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what operation is needed, then executes it. This cycle repeats billions of times per second on modern processors.

questions.question: What is the key difference between RAM and disk storage?
options: RAM is slower but persistent; disk is faster but volatile
RAM is fast but volatile; disk is slower but persistent
RAM and disk have the same speed but different capacities
RAM stores programs; disk stores only media files
questions.explanation: RAM (Random Access Memory) is extremely fast but loses all data when power is cut — it's volatile. Disk storage (HDD/SSD) is much slower but retains data without power — it's persistent. This tradeoff fundamentally shapes system design.

questions.question: What is a process in the context of an operating system?
options: A single CPU instruction being executed
A running program with its own isolated memory space
A physical core on the CPU chip
A file stored on disk waiting to be opened
questions.explanation: A process is a running instance of a program. The operating system gives each process its own isolated memory space, so one process cannot directly access or corrupt another's memory. This isolation is a fundamental OS protection mechanism.

questions.question: How do threads differ from processes?
options: Threads are always faster than processes
Threads within the same process share memory, while processes have isolated memory
Threads run on disk, processes run in RAM
There is no difference; they are the same concept
questions.explanation: Threads are lightweight execution units within a process. Unlike separate processes, threads share the same memory space, making communication between them fast but also making them prone to concurrency issues like race conditions.

questions.question: What is a context switch, and why does it have a cost?
options: Switching between programming languages at runtime, which requires recompilation
The OS saving one process's state and loading another's, which takes CPU cycles and disrupts caches
Physically swapping RAM sticks between motherboard slots
Changing the screen resolution, which forces the GPU to re-render
questions.explanation: A context switch occurs when the OS saves the current process's registers, program counter, and state, then loads another process's state. This costs CPU cycles and often flushes CPU caches, meaning the newly loaded process starts with cold caches.

questions.question: Why can't we simply replace all disk storage with RAM?
options: RAM is volatile (loses data on power loss) and costs significantly more per gigabyte than disk
RAM is actually slower than modern SSDs
Operating systems cannot address more than 4 GB of RAM
RAM chips are physically larger than disk drives
questions.explanation: RAM loses all data when power is removed, so it cannot serve as permanent storage without battery backup. Additionally, RAM costs roughly 30-50x more per gigabyte than SSD storage, making it economically impractical for large data sets.

questions.question: What primary role does the operating system play in managing hardware resources?
options: It compiles source code into machine instructions
It arbitrates access to CPU, memory, and I/O devices among competing processes
It physically repairs hardware faults in the CPU
It provides internet connectivity to all applications
questions.explanation: The operating system is a resource manager. It schedules CPU time among processes, allocates and protects memory regions, manages I/O device access, and provides abstractions (files, sockets) so applications don't manage hardware directly.

questions.question: A system has 4 CPU cores and 20 active processes. How does the OS create the illusion that all processes run simultaneously?
options: It queues 16 processes and only runs 4 at a time, with no switching
It rapidly context-switches between processes, giving each a small time slice on a core
It compresses all 20 processes into 4 combined processes
It uses RAM as extra CPU cores
questions.explanation: The OS scheduler assigns each process a short time slice (typically 1-10 ms) on a CPU core. When the slice expires, the OS context-switches to another process. This rapid switching — thousands of times per second — creates the illusion of simultaneous execution even with more processes than cores.

questions.question: Accessing data from L1 cache takes ~1 ns, RAM ~100 ns, and SSD ~100,000 ns. If a program repeatedly accesses a small dataset that fits in L1 cache, roughly how many times faster is it compared to reading from SSD each time?
options: About 10 times faster
About 1,000 times faster
About 100,000 times faster
About 1,000,000 times faster
questions.explanation: L1 cache access is ~1 ns while SSD access is ~100,000 ns, making L1 cache roughly 100,000 times faster. This enormous speed gap is why CPU caches exist and why cache-friendly data access patterns are critical for performance.

questions.question: A server process spawns 1,000 threads, each needing 1 MB of stack space. What is the minimum RAM consumed just by thread stacks, and what problem might this cause?
options: 1 MB total; no problem since threads share memory
1 GB total; this may exhaust available memory and cause excessive context switching
1,000 MB of disk space; threads use disk for stacks
Zero; modern OSes use virtual threads with no stack overhead
questions.explanation: Each thread gets its own stack, so 1,000 threads x 1 MB = 1 GB of RAM just for stacks. This doesn't include heap memory or other overhead. Beyond memory pressure, 1,000 threads cause heavy context-switching overhead, which is why event-driven and thread-pool architectures are preferred for high-concurrency servers.
